summary: IPv6 puts optional information in extension headers between the IPv6 and transport headers. This RFC describes issues in defining new extension headers, alternatives, and a common format for new ones.

eli5.summary: IPv6 messages can have extra labelled boxes inside. This gives one standard way to build new boxes so everyone can read their size.

questions: how to define new ipv6 extension header
what is the format of a new ipv6 extension header
why avoid new ipv6 extension headers
ipv6 destination options vs extension header
subtitle: Rules for when to invent a new IPv6 extension header, and one shared layout so middleboxes can skip it safely.

tldr.problem: Some deployed IPv6 routers and firewalls parse past all known extension headers at wire speed, so any new extension header can break them. Headers with hop-by-hop behavior can also be abused to attack routers.
tldr.mechanism: New extension headers are strongly discouraged in favor of destination options, and any that are created MUST start with a Next Header byte and a Hdr Ext Len byte, so a device can skip them without understanding them.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 2460 and sets the common format for future headers. It leaves several inspection problems unresolved and does not apply to existing headers such as the fragment header.

facts.label: Hdr Ext Len
facts.value: 8-bit, in 8-octet units, excluding the first 8 octets

today: RFC 6564 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2460. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem with New Extension Headers
sections.content:
IPv6 (RFC 2460) carries optional internet-layer information in extension headers placed between the IPv6 header and the transport header. Except for the Hop-by-Hop Options header, they are not usually processed by intermediate nodes.

In practice, several deployed routers and firewalls parse past or ignore all currently defined extension headers to look at transport-layer fields, which goes against RFC 2460. Some do it at wire speed with custom ASICs. So any new extension header risks breaking those deployments.

Headers or options with hop-by-hop behavior can also be subverted to attack the routers that process them. Field reports say some routers in the global Internet ignore such headers or drop packets that carry them.
sections.eli5: Some mail sorters have learned to skip every kind of box they know. A brand new kind of box could jam them, and a box every sorter must open could be used to cause trouble.

sections.title: When to Create a New Header
sections.content:
RFC 2460 allows both extension headers and destination options to carry optional destination information. Destination options give more flexible handling and better backward compatibility, so implementations SHOULD use them first and a new extension header only if they do not meet the need. A request for a new extension header MUST explain why destination options could not be used.

The base standard defines 3 extension headers for new IPv6 options (Routing, Destination Options and Hop-by-Hop Options), and allows new extension headers only in limited circumstances.

  • New extension headers with hop-by-hop behavior MUST NOT be created or specified.
  • New options for the existing Hop-by-Hop Header SHOULD NOT be created unless no alternative is feasible, and a proposal MUST explain why hop-by-hop behavior is absolutely essential.
  • New extension headers MUST NOT be created unless no existing one can carry the information as a new option, and the proposal MUST explain why.
sections.eli5: The rule is to use the boxes that already exist whenever you can. You need a very good written reason to make a new kind.

sections.title: The Uniform Header Layout
sections.content:
Any extension header defined in the future MUST use one consistent format, to minimize breakage in intermediate nodes that examine these headers. It begins with two bytes and then header-specific data.

  • Next Header: an 8-bit selector identifying the type of header that follows. It uses the same values as the IPv4 Protocol field.
  • Hdr Ext Len: an 8-bit unsigned integer giving the length of the extension header in 8-octet units, not including the first 8 octets.
  • Header Specific Data: variable length, defined by each header.

With these two fields in a known place, a node that does not understand the header can still compute where it ends and read the next one.
sections.eli5: Every new box must have a label at the front saying what is in the next box and how big this one is. Then anyone can skip it without opening it.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content: The scheme is not backward compatible with all currently defined extension headers. It applies only to newly defined ones. The fragment header predates this document and does not follow the format.
sections.eli5: The new labelling rule is only for boxes made from now on. The old boxes, like the fragment box, stay as they were.

sections.title: Unresolved Problems
sections.content:
The RFC calls this one step in easing inspection of extension headers by middleboxes, and says more work is needed. It lists issues left open:

  • There can be an arbitrary number of extension headers.
  • Extension headers must be processed in the order they appear.
  • Extension headers may alter the processing of the payload itself, so the packet may not be processed properly without knowing the header.
sections.eli5: Skipping boxes is easier now, but a pile of many boxes is still a lot to get through, and some boxes change what the contents mean.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: A standard format minimizes breakage at intermediate nodes that inspect but do not understand these headers. The cost is a risk: nodes such as firewalls that skip over unknown headers might end up allowing a covert channel from outside the firewall to the inside, using the data fields of the unknown headers.
sections.eli5: A guard who waves through boxes he does not understand might let someone sneak a secret message in one of them.

fields.name: Next Header
fields.desc: Type of the header that follows; same values as the IPv4 Protocol field.

fields.name: Hdr Ext Len
fields.desc: Length in 8-octet units, not counting the first 8 octets.

fields.name: Header Specific Data
fields.desc: Variable length; fields specific to this header.
